paragraphs: This paper studies how to answer graph clustering questions without processing the entire graph for every answer. The goal is an oracle: after an initial preparation stage, it can report which cluster a queried vertex belongs to. Both preparation and answering must take sublinear time, meaning less than time proportional to the graph’s size.

The analysis assumes strong cluster structure. Each hidden cluster has strong internal connectivity, expressed through large inner conductance, and relatively weak connections outward, expressed through small outer conductance. Answers must agree with a single partition that is close to the underlying clustering, so individually fast answers also form a coherent overall assignment.

Earlier approaches required either a demanding separation between internal and external connectivity or preprocessing exponential in relevant clustering parameters. The proposed algorithm relaxes these requirements while accepting a slightly larger misclassification ratio. The authors also establish robustness to a few random edge deletions and test their theoretical bounds on synthetic networks. The contribution is therefore a qualified efficiency improvement for strongly clusterable graphs.
neurips-2023-a-sublinear-time-spectral-c.tldr: A spectral clustering oracle reduces preprocessing requirements for strongly clusterable graphs while accepting slightly more misclassification.

paragraphs: Estimating where a species lives can require many field observations. This paper asks how to choose observation locations so that a limited number of visits reveals as much as possible about an unmapped species. Its approach combines information transferred from other species with active learning, which selects new observations based on current uncertainty.

The method represents the unknown range as a weighted combination of estimated ranges for other species. Models trained on large collections of community observations supply these candidate ranges, even though those observations provide weak supervision. The querying procedure then sequentially chooses geographic locations expected to reduce uncertainty about the target species’ range.

The authors evaluate the approach using expert-derived ranges for one thousand species. It outperforms the alternative active learning methods tested and approaches the performance of end-to-end trained models while using only a fraction of the data. These results support using crowdsourced observations both to build spatial representations and to guide further discovery. The value lies in turning existing observations into better choices about where to look next.
neurips-2023-active-learning-based-speci.tldr: The method transfers range information from other species to choose informative field visits and estimate an unmapped species’ distribution efficiently.

paragraphs: Online learning to rank repeatedly presents an ordered list of items and learns from user clicks. This paper investigates how an attacker can steer that learning process toward a chosen item. The central question is whether a relatively small cumulative attack cost can produce a persistent distortion in what the system selects.

The analysis begins with a UCB algorithm for stochastic bandits with binary feedback. This setting creates difficulties because feedback is both bounded and discrete. After addressing those difficulties, the authors construct attacks on UCB-based ranking algorithms under position-based and cascade click models. They also introduce a general strategy against any algorithm within the general click model studied.

Each proposed attack makes the learner choose the target item T minus o(T) times while paying a cumulative cost of o(T). In plain language, as the interaction horizon grows, the target is selected on an overwhelming fraction of rounds while average attack cost vanishes. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the attacks’ effectiveness. The results expose a strong vulnerability within the analyzed feedback settings.
neurips-2023-adversarial-attacks-on-onli.tldr: The paper develops attacks that steer online ranking learners toward a target item on nearly all rounds at sublinear cumulative cost.

paragraphs: Differentially private training commonly clips each example’s gradient, limiting its contribution to an update. Choosing the clipping threshold matters for accuracy, but adds a tuning burden. This paper proposes automatic clipping as a replacement that removes the need to tune that threshold across optimizers including DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-LAMB.

The automatic versions preserve the privacy and computational efficiency of existing private optimizers. The authors describe them as requiring no privacy-specific optimization hyperparameters, making the training procedure easier to use alongside familiar optimization methods. This matters because the contribution addresses a practical source of complexity in applying private learning, rather than merely offering another threshold-selection procedure.

The theoretical analysis covers automatic DP-SGD for nonconvex optimization. Under a symmetric noise assumption on per-example gradients, its asymptotic convergence rate can match ordinary SGD. That condition is essential to interpreting the rate claim. Across the language and vision tasks evaluated, automatic clipping matches or exceeds the reported state of the art. The authors also report that adopting it requires only small changes to existing implementations.
neurips-2023-automatic-clipping-differen.tldr: Automatic clipping removes clipping-threshold tuning from private optimizers while retaining privacy and reporting competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Visual object trackers distinguish a target object from its surrounding background as video progresses. The paper examines a vulnerability in trackers that extract positive and negative examples to learn that distinction. Its central finding is that poisoning a small portion of training data can introduce a backdoor through this example-selection process.

BadTrack places a predefined trigger in the background regions of training video frames. Because of where it appears, the trigger occurs almost exclusively among extracted negative examples. The attack therefore exploits the relationship between spatial placement and the training examples produced by the tracker. The proposed threat requires poisoning data rather than modifying the tracker through another intervention.

Experiments cover both two-stream Siamese trackers and one-stream Transformer trackers. The attack substantially reduces performance on poisoned data while leaving performance on clean data comparable to benign trackers. That combination matters because clean-data quality alone would not reveal the reported degradation. The authors present this as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration of a poison-only backdoor threat against visual object tracking.
neurips-2023-badtrack-a-poison-only-back.tldr: BadTrack poisons a small amount of tracking data to create a backdoor that degrades poisoned-data performance while preserving clean-data performance.

paragraphs: Determinant maximization selects k vectors whose associated volume is as large as possible. It provides a mathematical way to model diversity and is also the maximum-probability inference problem for determinantal point processes. For large datasets, the paper studies composable coresets: smaller selections that can be combined while retaining an approximation guarantee.

The main result strengthens the theoretical case for the widely used greedy algorithm. Its composable coreset approximation factor improves from the previously established C^(k²) guarantee to O(k)^(3k). The authors describe this as almost optimal relative to the known optimal scale of Õ(k)^k. This supports earlier experimental evidence that greedy selection is practical in this setting.

The proof centers on a local property: replacing one selected vector with an unselected vector can increase volume by at most a factor of 1 + √k. This bound is tight apart from the additive one. On real datasets, the experiments find smaller local improvement factors than the worst-case bound allows. The theoretical and empirical findings together explain why a simple greedy construction can produce useful summaries for diversity selection.
neurips-2023-composable-coresets-for-det.tldr: A sharper analysis shows that greedy selection yields almost-optimal composable coresets for determinant maximization.

paragraphs: Self-training expands a small labeled dataset by assigning predicted labels to unlabeled examples and then learning from them. These predictions, called pseudo-labels, can make additional data useful, but their accuracy strongly affects the result. This paper introduces a loss designed to balance reliance on pseudo-labels with reliance on the original labeled examples.

The method has provable behavior at two extremes. If the pseudo-labels are entirely wrong, it reduces to training only on labeled data. If they are completely correct, it becomes training on both labeled and pseudo-labeled data, increasing the effective sample size. These endpoint properties explain the intended robustness: the method can retain the labeled-data training process or exploit the larger dataset when the pseudo-labels support it.

The authors evaluate the doubly-robust loss on ImageNet image classification and nuScenes 3D object detection. In those experiments, it outperforms the self-training baseline. The contribution combines theoretical endpoint guarantees with evidence across two different prediction tasks. Its stated findings show a way to make the usefulness of additional unlabeled data depend more carefully on the quality of the labels assigned to it.
neurips-2023-doubly-robust-self-training.tldr: Doubly-robust self-training has provable fallback and full-data behavior at the extremes of pseudo-label accuracy and improves the tested self-training baseline.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning searches for training settings that improve a model’s performance. When the underlying data are sensitive, that search can itself create privacy risks, even when individual models are trained privately. This paper focuses on making the optimization process private while allowing it to learn from the outcomes of earlier trials.

The abstract contrasts the existing private approach of uniformly sampling settings at random with adaptive methods commonly used outside private learning. Adaptive search chooses its next candidate using information from previous outputs. DP-HyPO provides a framework for bringing that feedback-driven approach into private hyperparameter optimization, addressing the gap between the two settings.

The authors supply a differential privacy analysis of the framework and evaluate it on several real-world datasets. Their empirical results support its effectiveness. The significance is that privacy analysis extends to an adaptive tuning procedure, rather than stopping at the training of each candidate model. This makes the search strategy itself part of the private learning design and supports using information from earlier trials when selecting later ones.
neurips-2023-dp-hypo-an-adaptive-private.tldr: DP-HyPO enables adaptive hyperparameter search with a differential privacy analysis and empirical support on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A model’s overall performance can conceal groups of examples on which it performs poorly. Finding those groups is called slice discovery. This paper argues that a useful slice should also be coherent: the mistakes within it should occur for the same reason. Grouping failures together is more informative when they share an underlying explanation.

The proposed method, InfEmbed, uses influence functions to represent how training data affect individual test examples. These representations are called influence embeddings. It then applies K-Means clustering to them. Examples end up together because the training data influence them similarly, which is how the method satisfies the paper’s formalized coherence requirement.

InfEmbed outperforms the current leading methods on two benchmarks and supports model debugging in several case studies. These findings connect a simple clustering procedure with a more targeted representation of model behavior. The important design choice is what gets clustered: patterns of training-data influence provide a basis for identifying related errors. That makes the discovered groups potentially useful for understanding a shared failure mechanism, as illustrated by the debugging studies.
neurips-2023-error-discovery-by-clusteri.tldr: InfEmbed clusters test examples by training-data influence to discover coherent groups of model errors.

paragraphs: User models infer characteristics such as preferences from observed behavior. That behavior can also carry information about sensitive attributes, so excluding explicit sensitive labels does not prevent a model from learning related biases. Existing fairness approaches often try to decorrelate user representations from sensitive attributes, but many assume those attributes are labeled throughout the training data.

FairLISA addresses the more practical setting where sensitive labels are available for only some users. The authors first develop a theoretical connection between the fairness objective and data with both known and unknown sensitive attributes. They then use that connection to construct a general adversarial training framework that can draw on the full user dataset.

Experiments cover recommendation and cognitive diagnosis, with different proportions of missing sensitive labels. FairLISA improves fairness while retaining high accuracy in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore an approach to fair user modeling that can use partially labeled sensitive information. Its results support including users with unknown sensitive attributes in the fairness training process, rather than making complete sensitive-attribute annotation a prerequisite.
neurips-2023-fairlisa-fair-user-modeling.tldr: FairLISA uses users with both known and unknown sensitive attributes to improve fairness while retaining high accuracy in tested user-modeling tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether changing a language model’s internal activity while it answers can make its responses more truthful. Its technique, Inference-Time Intervention, learns directions associated with truthfulness and shifts activations along those directions in a limited set of attention heads. The adjustment happens during inference, when the model produces an answer.

On the TruthfulQA benchmark, the intervention substantially improves LLaMA models. For Alpaca, an instruction-tuned LLaMA, reported truthfulness rises from 32.5% to 65.1%. The authors also identify a tradeoff with helpfulness: increasing intervention strength is not simply an unrestricted improvement. Tuning that strength provides a way to balance the two properties.

The method is described as computationally inexpensive and minimally invasive, with only a few hundred examples needed to locate the relevant directions. These results suggest that a model may internally represent information about whether something is true even when its generated answer is false. That is an interpretation supported by the intervention findings, rather than proof that the model possesses a universally reliable internal truth detector.
neurips-2023-inference-time-intervention.tldr: Shifting selected attention-head activations improves measured truthfulness in LLaMA models, with intervention strength controlling a tradeoff with helpfulness.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often need to operate on graphs whose sizes differ from those seen during training. This paper studies when their behavior can transfer across such graphs. Earlier theoretical work used graph limits such as graphons, but those results applied meaningfully only to dense graphs, leaving important sparse settings outside their scope.

The authors instead study limits of operators derived from graphs, including the aggregation operations used by graph neural networks. This leads to graphops, a limit framework that accommodates sparse structures such as bounded-degree and power-law graphs. Focusing on the operators provides a way to compare the computations performed on different graph sizes.

The paper derives quantitative distance bounds between a finite graph neural network and its infinite-graph limit, as well as between networks evaluated on different-sized graphs with shared structural properties. The guarantees require a regularity assumption, which the authors verify for various graph sequences. The results cover dense and sparse graphs and several graph-limit notions. They establish conditional control over size transfer rather than unrestricted generalization to arbitrary new graphs.
neurips-2023-limits-approximation-and-si.tldr: An operator-based analysis gives conditional bounds on graph neural network approximation and size transfer for both sparse and dense graphs.

paragraphs: Multi-exit networks can return predictions before completing all their computation, making inference more efficient. Their exits, however, depend heavily on related submodels. An adversarial example aimed at one exit can therefore harm other exits as well. This paper targets that cross-exit vulnerability while preserving the efficiency motivation for using early predictions.

NEO-KD combines two knowledge-distillation components within adversarial training. Neighbor knowledge distillation guides predictions on adversarial examples toward the combined predictions of nearby exits on clean data. Exit-wise orthogonal knowledge distillation is intended to reduce how readily adversarial examples transfer between submodels. The two components address both the quality of attacked predictions and the coupling of vulnerabilities across exits.

Across the datasets and models tested, NEO-KD improves robustness and achieves the best adversarial accuracy among the compared approaches under reduced computation budgets. Those comparisons include existing adversarial-training and knowledge-distillation techniques for multi-exit networks. The findings support designing robustness training around the relationships among exits: a network that offers multiple stopping points also needs to account for how an attack can affect those points together.
neurips-2023-neo-kd-knowledge-distillati.tldr: NEO-KD uses two distillation mechanisms to improve adversarial robustness and reduce attack transfer across a network’s early exits.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, but their usual generation process may require hundreds of iterations. Distillation aims to replace that long process with a faster model. This paper tackles two stated difficulties of earlier approaches: complicated training procedures with multiple stages and weak performance when generation is reduced to a single step.

The proposed student architecture is the Generative Equilibrium Transformer, or GET, a new deep equilibrium model. It learns a direct mapping from initial noise to the corresponding image produced by a diffusion model. Training can happen entirely offline using stored noise-image pairs, so the training data directly describe the mapping the student is meant to reproduce.

With comparable training budgets, the approach outperforms existing one-step methods in the reported evaluation. GET also matches the FID scores of a Vision Transformer five times larger. The authors identify the equilibrium architecture as crucial to this result. The contribution combines a straightforward distillation setup with an architecture that achieves a favorable balance between computational cost and image quality in the tested one-step generation setting.
neurips-2023-one-step-diffusion-distilla.tldr: GET distills diffusion-generated noise-image pairs into a one-step generator that outperforms compared methods at similar training budgets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces ProBio as an initial step toward intelligent monitoring of molecular biology experiments. Its motivation is the difficulty of reproducing research results. To study how automated systems might understand laboratory activity, the authors create a multimodal dataset with detailed annotations organized into a hierarchy of activities.

The dataset supports two benchmarks tailored to laboratory work: tracking transparent solutions and recognizing actions using multiple modalities. These tasks emphasize that understanding a biology experiment involves challenges specific to the setting. The hierarchical annotations give researchers a structured basis for studying laboratory activity at a fine level of detail, while the benchmarks define concrete problems on which systems can be evaluated.

The authors evaluate contemporary video-understanding models and identify limitations in their performance in this specialized domain. The contribution is a research resource and an assessment of current capabilities, presented as groundwork for monitoring systems. It does not establish that automated monitoring has solved reproducibility problems. Instead, the findings identify laboratory activity understanding as an area where existing video methods need further development.
neurips-2023-probio-a-protocol-guided-mu.tldr: ProBio supplies annotated laboratory data and two benchmarks to study activity understanding as groundwork for intelligent experiment monitoring.

paragraphs: RAPHAEL is a text-conditioned diffusion model designed to generate artistic images that reflect prompts containing multiple objects, attributes, and actions. Its central architectural idea is to stack many mixture-of-experts layers across space and diffusion time. Their combinations create billions of possible routes through the network.

The authors describe each route intuitively as a painter responsible for a textual concept in a particular image region at a particular diffusion timestep. This connects the architecture to the challenge of depicting several parts of a prompt together. The reported experiments also examine the model’s ability to produce different styles, including comics, realism, cyberpunk, and ink illustration.

The evaluated model has three billion parameters and was trained using 1,000 A100 GPUs for two months. It achieves a zero-shot COCO FID of 6.61, reported as state of the art, and outperforms the compared systems in ViLG-300 human evaluation. The authors also report stronger image quality and aesthetic appeal than the named competing models. These findings support the proposed mixture architecture within the substantial training setup described.
neurips-2023-raphael-text-to-image-gener.tldr: RAPHAEL combines spatial and temporal expert layers into many diffusion routes, reporting strong text-to-image quality and aesthetic results.

paragraphs: Breaking a problem into intermediate steps can help language models reason, but longer chains also create opportunities for uncertainty and mistakes to accumulate. This paper introduces a mechanism that evaluates reasoning step by step. Those evaluations guide which developing reasoning paths the model explores as it searches for an answer.

The decoding algorithm combines self-evaluation with stochastic beam search. Self-evaluation supplies an automatic criterion for judging intermediate reasoning, while temperature-controlled randomness balances following promising paths with exploring alternatives. The approach makes assessment part of the search process, so the model can use intermediate judgments when choosing how to continue a chain.

For Codex-based systems, the authors report few-shot accuracy improvements of 6.34%, 9.56%, and 5.46% over the corresponding baselines on GSM8K, AQuA, and StrategyQA. Llama-2 arithmetic experiments also show improvements over baselines at comparable computational budgets. Further analysis finds that the guidance identifies logical failures and improves consistency and robustness. These results support stepwise evaluation as a useful search signal in the tested multi-step reasoning tasks.
neurips-2023-self-evaluation-guided-beam.tldr: Stepwise self-evaluation guides stochastic beam search toward more accurate and consistent language-model reasoning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Piecewise affine systems describe behavior using different affine rules in different regions. They are useful for studying dynamics that change sharply, as can occur in control and robotics. The difficulty is that crossing between regions can introduce discontinuities. In general sequential settings, those discontinuities make learning impossible, leaving practical approaches dependent on heuristics.

This paper uses smoothed online learning to obtain guarantees under a weak smoothness assumption. Within that setting, the authors provide prediction and simulation algorithms whose regret is polynomial in all relevant problem parameters. They also establish efficiency in the number of calls made to an optimization oracle. The smoothness condition is central to moving beyond the unrestricted impossibility.

The results apply to both one-step prediction and multi-step simulation of piecewise affine dynamical systems. For simulation, the learner generates trajectories, and regret is measured using Wasserstein distance between simulated and true data. This connects the theory to discrepancies between entire trajectory distributions. The contribution supplies a principled, conditional basis for learning systems with abrupt changes, together with technical tools the authors identify as more broadly useful.
neurips-2023-smoothed-online-learning-fo.tldr: Under a weak smoothness assumption, the paper gives oracle-efficient prediction and simulation algorithms with polynomial regret for piecewise affine systems.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks have attracted interest for energy-efficient visual recognition, but their use for 3D point clouds has received less attention. This paper introduces Spiking PointNet to explore that setting. It identifies two obstacles: difficulty optimizing large spiking models over many time steps, and PointNet’s substantial memory and computational requirements.

The proposed approach separates the time-step choices used during training and inference. Spiking PointNet trains with a single time step, then can use multiple time steps when making predictions. The authors provide theoretical justification and experimental analysis showing that this strategy can perform better than directly training with multiple time steps, while avoiding that more demanding training setup.

Experiments on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The model can even outperform its conventional artificial-neural-network counterpart in the reported evaluation, alongside training speedups and storage savings. The findings suggest that using more temporal computation at inference need not require equally extensive temporal computation during training. This provides a potential direction for making spiking models practical for point-cloud recognition, with the stated benefits supported by the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2023-spiking-pointnet-spiking-ne.tldr: Spiking PointNet trains with one time step and uses multiple steps at inference to improve point-cloud recognition while reducing training costs.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can depend on cues that frequently accompany a class without being reliable evidence of it. This paper measures that reliance by sorting images within each class according to how strongly such cues appear. An interpretable network’s deep features provide a proxy for this degree of spuriosity.

The rankings identify low-spuriosity minority groups and allow bias to be measured as the accuracy difference between high- and low-spuriosity images. They also guide a mitigation procedure: finetuning the classification head on low-spuriosity examples. The authors report that this can remove the measured bias with little loss of accuracy, using images already available in the dataset.

On ImageNet, the work annotates 5,000 class-feature dependencies, identifies 630 as spurious, and produces 325,000 soft feature segmentations. Evaluating 89 models reveals that class-specific biases are highly correlated across models. This pattern suggests that training data influence spurious-feature reliance much more strongly than the training approach does. The interpretation remains a conclusion suggested by those comparisons, while the rankings provide a concrete method for inspecting and addressing the measured dependence.
neurips-2023-spuriosity-rankings-sorting.tldr: Ranking images by spurious-cue strength reveals classifier biases and enables inexpensive mitigation through classification-head finetuning.

paragraphs: Robust binary classification seeks correct decisions even when an adversary can alter each input within a small neighborhood. Its natural objective counts classification errors under those perturbations. Training commonly substitutes another loss for this zero-one objective, raising a theoretical question: does optimizing the replacement still lead toward the intended robust classification objective?

The paper gives a complete characterization of surrogate losses that satisfy adversarial consistency for any data distribution. Here, consistency concerns minimizing sequences: progressively optimizing the surrogate must preserve the relevant connection to minimizing the original adversarial risk. The result identifies exactly which replacement losses meet this distribution-independent requirement in the setting studied.

The authors also prove a quantitative consistency result for the rho-margin loss, strengthening the qualitative relationship for that particular surrogate. Their characterization shows that adversarially consistent losses form a substantially smaller class than consistent losses in ordinary classification. Consequently, a surrogate’s established suitability without adversarial perturbations does not by itself establish its suitability for robust learning. The contribution clarifies the mathematical requirements behind choosing a replacement objective for adversarial training.
neurips-2023-the-adversarial-consistency.tldr: The paper completely characterizes distribution-independent adversarially consistent surrogate losses and shows they are more restricted than ordinary consistent losses.

paragraphs: The Cambridge Law Corpus provides a large collection of UK court cases for legal AI research. It contains more than 250,000 cases, mainly from the twenty-first century, with some dating back to the sixteenth century. The initial release includes the original case text and metadata, giving researchers both document content and accompanying descriptive information.

The authors also supply legal-expert annotations of outcomes for 638 cases. These annotations support a concrete evaluation task: extracting the outcome expressed in a case. Using that annotated subset, the paper trains and evaluates GPT-3, GPT-4, and RoBERTa models to establish benchmarks. This connects the broader document collection to a defined task with expert-provided reference annotations.

Because court materials can contain sensitive information, the paper includes an extensive legal and ethical discussion. The resulting release is restricted to research use under specified conditions. Those restrictions are part of how the resource is made available. The contribution combines scale, historical coverage, expert annotations, and benchmark evaluations to provide a foundation for studying legal text with AI.
neurips-2023-the-cambridge-law-corpus-a-.tldr: The Cambridge Law Corpus combines over 250,000 UK cases with expert outcome annotations and extraction benchmarks under restricted research access.

paragraphs: Transfer-based adversarial attacks exploit the possibility that an input designed to fool one model will also fool another. This makes them relevant when a target model’s architecture and parameters are unavailable. The paper examines how to compare these attacks fairly, arguing that inconsistent evaluation practices make their effectiveness difficult to assess.

The authors identify problems including unfair comparisons and insufficient coverage of possible substitute and victim models. A substitute model is used to construct the attack, while a victim model is the system on which it is tested. Considering both matters because an evaluation’s conclusions depend on the model choices used to demonstrate transfer.

To provide a more systematic basis for comparison, the paper introduces TA-Bench, which implements more than 30 attack methods. It evaluates them on ImageNet using 10 popular substitute or victim models. The study reports new insights into method effectiveness and provides guidance for future evaluations. Its main contribution is a shared evaluation framework and a broader comparative study, helping researchers assess attack claims against a more consistent experimental basis.
neurips-2023-towards-evaluating-transfer.tldr: TA-Bench compares more than 30 transfer-based attacks across 10 models to support more systematic and fair evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for the intuition that deep neural networks learn simpler concepts more readily than complex ones. It makes that question more precise by focusing on interactive concepts: collaborations among sets of input variables whose combined effects contribute to the network’s inference scores.

The starting point is earlier work showing that a network typically encodes only a small number of these interactive concepts and can be understood through their interaction effects. Within this perspective, complexity refers to how many input variables participate in a concept. A concept involving more variables represents a larger collaboration, giving the analysis a concrete notion of complexity to examine.

The paper’s stated finding explains why concepts involving more input variables are harder to learn and clarifies the conceptual complexity responsible for that difficulty. Its contribution is theoretical rather than a proposed training procedure or benchmark comparison. The explanation connects a particular structure inside network computations to learning difficulty. This gives the broad intuition about simple and complex concepts a more specific interpretation grounded in the number of jointly interacting inputs.
neurips-2023-towards-the-difficulty-for-.tldr: The paper theoretically connects greater learning difficulty to concepts that require interactions among more input variables.

paragraphs: Video stylization changes a video’s visual appearance while dealing with motion across frames. Applying an image stylization method independently to each frame is one approach. This paper instead investigates direct stylization with a 3D convolutional network, whose learned representations combine appearance with motion from both the camera and the subjects.

That entanglement makes a straightforward extension of 2D stylization methods ineffective in the setting studied. ViSt3D explicitly separates appearance and motion, applies stylization to the appearance component, then restores the motion component before decoding the final video. The design gives appearance transformation a distinct place in a representation that also contains temporal information.

The authors assemble a training dataset from existing datasets and independently collect a test set for examining generalization. On that test set, they compare their approach with 2D methods applied frame by frame and report better texture stylization. They present the work as, to their knowledge, the first direct use of a 3D CNN for video stylization. The results support disentangling appearance and motion as a route to successful stylization with such networks.
neurips-2023-vist3d-video-stylization-wi.tldr: ViSt3D separates appearance from motion in a 3D CNN and reports better texture stylization than frame-by-frame 2D methods.
